title: Quadkey to XYZ Tile Converter: Decode the Key
description: Decode a Bing quadkey into its XYZ tile numbers with the Quadkey to XYZ Tile Converter — zoom from length, x and y from the bits. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, quadkey 032010110132021 decodes to zoom 15, tile x 9649, y 12314 — Times Square's tile, recovered from a single string of digits 0–3.
quick_answer: The Quadkey to XYZ Tile Converter decodes a quadkey string into the tile it names: the zoom (the string's length) and the x and y tile numbers (its interleaved bits, unpicked). Paste a quadkey and read the XYZ address — the translation Bing-keyed data needs for the tile world.

Each quadkey digit contributes one bit to x and one to y, most significant first: digit 3 sets both bits, 1 sets x's, 2 sets y's, 0 sets neither. Fifteen digits unpick into x 9649 and y 12314 exactly.
'32010110132021' (a leading zero eaten by a spreadsheet) decodes to a zoom-14 tile in a different place — valid-looking, wholly wrong. Quadkeys are strings; treat them as strings.

faq: How long can a quadkey be?
Bing's system defines up to 23 digits (zoom 23). Real datasets rarely pass the high teens — each digit quadruples the tile count.
Anything outside 0–3 is not a quadkey digit — the converter flags it rather than guessing. Letters mean you are holding a geohash or another system entirely.
Leading zeros lost in my spreadsheet.
The classic injury. Pad left with zeros to the intended zoom if you know it; if you do not, the decode is ambiguous between zooms — a data-loss lesson the whole industry has learned once.
Quadkeys are defined on the XYZ (unflipped) grid. TMS-derived keys need their y un-flipped before or after decoding — know your source stack.
